name: Silas Crane
hook: A Blue Ridge farrier who still runs a coal forge behind his barn.
tell: He gives the anvil horn two light hammer taps before he speaks.
story:
Silas Crane works a coal forge behind his barn in the Blue Ridge, the kind of shop where the floor is packed dirt and scale, the anvil sits in a ring of scorch marks, and the radio, when it is on, is turned down low. Neighbors still trailer horses to him for shoes, and he will repair a broken hinge or a wagon iron if you leave it by the door. He learned the work from his father and never saw a reason to switch the fire to propane. He talks in an unhurried Appalachian baritone, and he does not fill a silence just to be polite.

In the late afternoon he often stands in the barn door with a rag in his hand and watches the light go off the ridge. He will not make a speech about any of that. He will say the shoe is tight enough, the coal is burning clean, and if you wait he will finish the last tap.
identity_block: Silas Crane, a man in his 60s, about 5 feet 11 inches tall, solid through the chest and forearms from a lifetime at the anvil, a slight working stoop in the shoulders, thick-knuckled weathered hands with stained nail beds and a few old nicks. A long weathered rectangular face with a high forehead, deep nasolabial folds, crow's feet, a softly squared jaw hidden by the beard, a straight medium-wide nose with a faint bump on the bridge slightly left of center from an old break, a thin closed mouth, and natural asymmetry (the left eye a touch more hooded, the right brow sitting a little lower). Weathered fair-ruddy skin, sun-darkened on the forehead and cheekbones and paler under the beard, uneven tone, a few small age spots at the temples, visible pores, broken capillaries on the nose and cheeks, and under-eye bags. Pale gray-blue eyes, deep-set, slightly watery, heavy lids, bushy mixed silver-and-dark brows, natural lashes, no sparkly catchlights — only a small dim natural highlight if any. Fictional original face, not a likeness of any real person or celebrity. Three visible locks only: (1) thinning close-cropped silver-white hair, receding at both temples, short and sparse on top with the scalp visible through the hair, no comb-over, no hat, and the same sparse length from behind ending well above the collar — keep the hair sparse like the locked front headshot, not a full thick white cap; a full short silver-white beard about two inches long, neatly kept but not salon-trimmed, slightly uneven at the edges, with a darker steel-gray streak only through the chin and the center of the mustache, not the cheeks; (2) a short pale nick-scar on the right cheek just above the beard line, about a fingernail long — in a front view it sits on the left side of the photo; in a view that shows his left side it is on the far side and must be hidden, never flipped to the left cheek; if the scar cannot be placed correctly, hide it rather than flip it; (3) a faded pale thumbprint-sized burn scar on the outer right forearm just below the rolled sleeve, only when that forearm is visible, never on the left arm — in a front view the right forearm is on the left side of the photo; in a rear view the right forearm is on the right side of the photo; if the burn cannot be placed on the right forearm, hide it rather than flip it. Signature wardrobe: a worn brown leather farrier's apron, darkened and scorched at the belly, over a faded indigo chambray work shirt with the sleeves rolled to mid-forearm; heavy dark-brown canvas work pants; scuffed chestnut leather work boots. A faded rust shop rag often hangs from the apron pocket. No logos, no printed typography on clothes, tools, drawers, or walls. Photographed as a real person in candid, imperfect light: mixed 35mm documentary and phone-camera looks, harsh uneven practical forge and barn light, soot, sweat, a messy working shop, sensor noise, imperfect focus, natural skin, no catalog sheen, no beauty retouching, no CGI or plastic sheen.
